titel: The business model of the US financial industry
kurz: Which parties earn money from a US brokerage or retirement account, from which sources, and why the form of compensation shapes the recommendation.

bloecke.md:
A financial product has two prices. One appears on the trade confirmation; the other pays the parties behind it: fund sponsor, custodian, index provider, trading venue, broker and adviser. This second price is usually the larger one. It is designed so that it never appears as an invoice. The investor notices it only as a slightly lower return.

These costs are justified in principle, because custody, liquidity, settlement and advice are real services that cost money. A conflict of interest arises where the way payment is made decides which product is recommended. Assessing the industry therefore starts with the question of whom a product pays, and only then with the question of what it costs.

## The parties and their income

It starts with the fund sponsor. Its adviser manages the mutual fund or ETF and takes the management fee daily, pro rata, from the fund's assets. The investor does not transfer this fee; it shows only in a marginally lower share price. The **expense ratio** sums up this ongoing deduction. From the fund's assets, the fund also pays the custodian, which holds the securities, the transfer agent, which keeps the shareholder records, and the licence for the index it tracks. A second income arises from the client assets themselves, namely through securities lending. How the lending income is split between the fund and the sponsor or its lending agent is disclosed in the fund's statement of additional information.

Many mutual funds also pay **12b-1 fees** out of fund assets, named after the SEC rule that permits them. They finance distribution and ongoing service, and much of the money goes to the broker or adviser who sold the fund, every year for as long as the investor holds it. In addition, fund companies pay some brokers **revenue sharing** for a place on their platform.

The broker earns from commissions where they still exist, from the interest margin on uninvested cash, from margin loans and from [[Payment for order flow|payment for order flow]]. Wholesale [[Market maker|market makers]] that execute retail orders earn from the difference between bid and ask price, the spread, which is contained in the price rather than shown on the trade confirmation. With insurance products such as annuities, the insurer earns from the margin between what the contract costs it and what it charges, and pays the selling agent a commission.

bloecke.md: The table lacks a fourth column stating who pays in the end. It would have the same entry in every row: the investor. The industry distributes among itself money that comes from this one source.

A mutual fund in Class A shares is sold with a front-end load of 5.75% of the offering price. Of an investment of $10,000, $575 goes to the sales channel and $9,425 is invested. For larger amounts, the load falls at so-called breakpoints.

A broad index ETF with an expense ratio of 0.05% costs about $5 a year on $10,000. The load therefore equals more than a century of ongoing costs of such an ETF. It is paid all at once on purchase, that is before the first dollar of return has been earned.

## Legal separation of brokers and advisers

In the US, both models exist side by side, governed by different laws.

**Broker-dealers** and their registered representatives are supervised by the SEC and FINRA. They are mostly paid per transaction or product sale. Since 30 June 2020, Regulation Best Interest has required them to act in the client's best interest when they make a recommendation, and to disclose and mitigate conflicts of interest. Commissions remain permitted, and the duty applies at the moment of the recommendation, not as ongoing monitoring of the account.

**Registered investment advisers** (RIAs) are registered with the SEC or, if smaller, with their state. Under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940, they owe their clients a fiduciary duty of care and loyalty for the whole relationship. They are usually paid by the client, by the hour, as a flat fee or as a percentage of assets. Advisers who receive no compensation from product providers at all call themselves fee-only. The similar-sounding term fee-based usually means fees plus commissions.

Many firms and individuals are registered as both and can act as broker in one account and as adviser in another. Insurance agents who sell annuities are licensed and supervised by the states; most states have adopted a best-interest standard for annuity sales. Since 2020, broker-dealers and advisers must give retail clients a short relationship summary, Form CRS, that describes services, fees and conflicts. Disclosure is thus regulated. The conflict of interest nonetheless remains, because disclosure does not abolish the commissions.

bloecke.titel: Four forms of compensation and their incentives
bloecke.unter: The conflict of interest is created by tying compensation to a sale or a transaction, regardless of its amount.

felder.text: Paid by the client per trade or per contract. Revenue arises only when something is bought or sold. Rewards activity.
Front-end load, commission paid by the insurer. Revenue arises only when something is signed. Sales therefore need occasions.
Hourly, flat or project fee. The advice to change nothing is paid for here just like any other. An advisory fee on assets belongs here too, but rewards gathering assets.
Flow as long as the product stays in place. Reward holding rather than switching, but depend on volume, regardless of the quality of the advice.

bloecke.md:
With variable annuities, the insurer usually pays the selling agent's commission up front and recovers it through ongoing contract charges. If you leave early, a **surrender charge** applies, which is often around 7% in the first year and declines over six to eight years. On top come the mortality and expense risk charge, administrative fees, the costs of the underlying funds and optional riders. Withdrawals before age 59½ can additionally trigger a 10% federal tax penalty on the earnings.

Policyholders who surrender a variable annuity after three years therefore often get back considerably less than the account value suggests. This applies even if the funds within the contract have risen. An exchange into another annuity (a Section 1035 exchange) avoids tax, but often starts a new surrender period and pays a new commission.

## Effect of costs in the portfolio

Costs reduce the final value, including the return that the deducted amounts would have earned over the entire term. The monthly contribution is unaffected. The following illustrative calculation assumes $250 a month over 25 years and a 6% gross return before costs. A total of $75,000 is paid in.

bloecke.md:
A cross-check shows how much of this reaches the sales side. Over the term, $4,312.50 of loads are paid, most of which goes to the selling firm. If the 1% ongoing charges include a 12b-1 service fee of 0.25% a year, it adds up to around $3,472 in the same model. Together that is about $7,784 for advice for which the client never saw an invoice. At an hourly rate of $200, this would equal more than 38 hours of advice spread over 25 years. During that time most investors speak to their representative barely a dozen times.

Part of the damage, however, is borne by the IRS, because lost gains are not taxed either. In a taxable account, long-term gains are taxed at 15% for most investors, plus any state tax. After federal tax, the gross loss of $31,058 thus falls to roughly $26,400. In a traditional IRA or 401(k), withdrawals are taxed as ordinary income, so the reduction depends on the tax bracket in retirement. This does not change the order of magnitude.

## Sales incentives and product selection

Advisers whose income depends on a sale need occasions for sales. A broadly diversified index portfolio, a term life insurance policy and a high-yield savings account offer a single occasion and then none for decades. A thematic fund, a structured note, an annuity or a portfolio switch, by contrast, offer new occasions again and again.

This is rarely intentional; mostly it is a selection effect. Products with a margin finance sales, training, advertising and comparison sites. Products without a margin lack this support. That is why you hear a lot about the former and little about the latter. The reason is the compensation rather than the quality, because nobody earns money by pointing to a product without a margin.

On the other hand, commission-based sales reach people who would never pay a fee for advice, and inadequate insurance costs more than any commission. Fee-based advice costs visible money, rarely pays off for small sums and does not guarantee better answers. An advisory fee of 1% a year on assets is not a neutral price either: it grows with the account, whether or not any advice is given. The form of compensation says something about the incentives, but not everything about the quality of the advice.

schritte.titel: Ask for the compensation in dollars, one-off and ongoing
schritte.text: What you want is an amount in dollars, not a percentage and not a sentence like “the fund company pays me”. Form CRS and the prospectus describe the fees; ask for the figure for your amount. If the adviser cannot or will not name it promptly, that is a warning sign.

schritte.titel: Ask whether the adviser acts as a fiduciary at all times
schritte.text: Ask whether the person acts as a fiduciary for all recommendations and all accounts, or only for some. Check the person in FINRA BrokerCheck and in the SEC's Investment Adviser Public Disclosure database, including any disciplinary history.

schritte.titel: Ask about the rejected alternative and its costs
schritte.text: A sound recommendation includes a benchmark for comparison. If there is no comparison with a simple option, such as a broad index fund or a high-yield savings account, no alternatives were weighed and the product was merely sold.

schritte.titel: Ask what happens if you leave after three years
schritte.text: This question reveals surrender charges, contingent deferred sales charges and transfer fees. It also shows how long the product must be held for it to pay off for the investor.

bloecke.titel: Zero commissions and the debate on fiduciary rules
bloecke.md:
In October 2019, the large online brokers eliminated commissions on online trades in US stocks and ETFs. The brokers' need for revenue remained and shifted to interest margins on uninvested cash, payment for order flow, margin lending and product fees. With every change of this kind, when one source of income disappears, another one grows.

The EU took a different route and banned payment for order flow, with a transition period in Germany until 30 June 2026. In the US, it remains legal; the SEC's 2022 proposals that would have required many retail orders to be exposed to auctions were not adopted.

For retirement advice, the Department of Labor has tried several times to impose a broader fiduciary standard. A rule from 2016 was vacated by a federal appeals court in 2018, and a new rule from 2024 was stayed by federal courts shortly before it was due to take effect. For investors, this means the protection depends on who advises them in which role, not on the account type.

The question “What does this cost me?” is not enough on its own. More revealing is the question of who is paid for proposing this particular product, and from which money. In the US, Form CRS, the fund prospectus and Form ADV Part 2A must answer both; ask for them before you sign.

mitnehmen: Fund sponsor, custodian, index provider, broker, market maker and adviser are all paid from the same source: the investor's assets.
The conflict of interest arises from tying compensation to a sale or a transaction, regardless of its amount.
With $75,000 paid in, a 5.75% load plus 1% ongoing charges reduces the final value in the model by around $31,000 over 25 years.
Regulation Best Interest and Form CRS do not eliminate the conflict; they make it recognisable. Only registered investment advisers owe a fiduciary duty for the whole relationship.
If a source of revenue disappears, as commissions did in 2019, the need for revenue remains and shifts to other fees and margins.

begriffe.text: Annual fee charged to fund assets to pay for distribution and shareholder service, named after SEC Rule 12b-1. Much of it goes to the broker or adviser who sold the fund, for as long as the investor holds it.
One-off sales charge deducted from the purchase amount of a mutual fund, typically on Class A shares. It falls at breakpoints for larger amounts. FINRA rules cap sales charges at 8.5%.

SEC rule in force since 30 June 2020. Broker-dealers must act in the retail customer's best interest when making a recommendation and must disclose and mitigate conflicts. Commissions remain permitted.
Duty of care and loyalty that registered investment advisers owe their clients under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940, for the whole advisory relationship.
Charge for withdrawing money from an annuity or insurance contract during the first years. It typically declines year by year and allows the insurer to recover the commission paid up front.
